title: Leadership Stop Fighting the Operating Rules of Your Brain and Work Smarter Parker Houston
author: Houston, Parker
summary: Parker Houston argues the 'work harder and longer' approach violates the brain's fundamental operating principles, leading to exhaustion and diminishing returns. Four evidence-based strategies: applying the Pareto Principle to protect the highest-value 20% of work (since overwhelmed brains default to low-value tasks); scheduling the most important work during peak brain hours — typically 9am to noon — since decision quality degrades dramatically through the day (judges granted 65% of paroles at 8am vs. nearly zero by 4pm; doctors prescribed 26% more unnecessary antibiotics late in the day); scheduling consistent breaks following the 52-minute work / 17-minute break optimal ratio (Harvard research shows more than 10 vacation days per year increases raise probability 34%); and continuously eliminating low-value tasks despite the brain's natural additive bias — described by Leidy Klotz as the systematic human tendency to overlook subtractive solutions.
points: Most professionals attempt to violate their brain's operating system with the 'work harder and longer' approach — modern neuroscience and cognitive psychology explain why this is exhausting and ineffective.
Pareto Principle applied to work: when overwhelmed or exhausted, brains default to picking low-value work — explicitly naming what's most important each day is a countermeasure.
Decision quality degrades predictably: judges granted 65% of paroles at 8am vs. nearly zero by 4pm; doctors prescribed 26% more unnecessary antibiotics late in the day.
Optimal work-rest ratio: 52 minutes of work followed by a 17-minute break; more than 10 vacation days per year increases raise probability by 34%.
The brain has a natural additive bias that makes subtraction of low-value commitments counter-intuitive but essential — Leidy Klotz's Subtract documents this systematic blind spot.
quotes: Many of us are working in a way that attempts to violate the fundamental operating system principles of our brains. Today we are going to look at research from modern neuroscience and cognitive psychology that helps to explain why the way many of us work is often exhausting and ineffective.

The sheer number of potential choices and distractions we face in the modern world has increased to an insane level. And the busier we become, the worse we are at selecting the most important tasks. In fact, when we become overwhelmed or exhausted, our brains default to picking low value work.

One famous study in 2011 looked at judges and their decisions about whether to grant parole to prisoners. They found that the first prisoners seen by the judge at 8am in the morning had a 65% percent average chance of being granted parole. By the end of the day at 4pm, their chances of being paroled dwindled to almost zero.

Studies consistently show that when we fail to take breaks, our productivity and performance goes down. In an often-cited study, researchers found that 52 minutes working with a 17-minute break was ideal for productivity.

Professor Leidy Klotz has written an amazing and highly scientific book packed with studies about how our brain has a natural tendency toward additive solutions. In it, he masterfully demonstrates how the human brain systematically overlooks subtractive solutions.
